newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Chances of UN oil embargo against Libya remote.
newsitem.headline: Chances of UN oil embargo against Libya remote.

text.p: Chances of the Security Council imposing an oil embargo against Libya are remote, according to council envoys who have discussed the issue over the years.

A bipartisan group of 53 U.S. senators has sent a letter to Bill Richardson, the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, urging Washington to introduce a resolution in the Council to impose an international oil embargo against Libya.
The letter was prompted by pleas from families of the 270 people killed on Pam Am flight 103, which exploded over the Scottish village of Lockerbie in 1988.
The families, seeing years go by without the accused coming to trial, are expected to insist the United States take further unilateral steps if no action is undertaken in the council.
A key western diplomat said Richardson had not taken any action yet but that the chances of any oil embargo were "very slim. At the moment it is still a U.S. domestic initiative."
An Egyptian delegate told Reuters: "Europe is living on the oil. It would suffer more than Libya. No chance."
And China's spokesman Chen Ranfeng said, "Sanctions are not popular."
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright during her tenure as U.N. ambassador attempted several times to impose heavier sanctions against Libya but admitted there was little support for them.
In November 1993, sanctions were tightened to prohibit the sale of some oil-related equipment for refineries but not production equipment Libya needs to drill for oil.
This resolution also freezes Libya's financial assets abroad, including investments, stocks and dividends. But it excludes funds derived from oil, natural gas or agricultural commodities.

The Security Council in 1992 imposed an air and diplomatic embargo against Libya for refusing to surrender to Britain or the United States two suspects accused of carrying out the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103.
Libya also has to satisfy demands of a French magistrate investigating the mid-flight bombing of France's UTA Flight 772 over Niger in 1989 in which 171 people died.
